Generalisability weights for a trial

Source: R/gensw.R
gensw.Rd

The weights that make the units of a randomised trial stand for a target population, and how far the trial is from it. The data hold the trial's units (s = 1) and a sample of the target (s = 0) with the same covariates. The sampling score ps, the chance of being in the trial given the covariates, is a logistic regression of s on x, trimmed to [trim, 1 - trim].

Usage

gensw(data, s, x, target = c("generalize", "transport"), trim = 0, bins = 10)

# S3 method for class 'gensw'
print(x, ...)

Arguments

data

A data frame, one row per unit of the trial or the target.

s

The name of the column marking the trial's units: 1 in the trial, 0 outside it (or TRUE, FALSE), both present.

x

The names of the covariate columns (numbers) of the sampling model; for print(), an object of class gensw.

target

"generalize" or "transport".

trim

The bound of the scores, from 0 to below 0.5.

bins

The bins of Tipton's index: a whole number from 1 to 10000.

...

Not used by print().

Value

An object of class gensw, a list: ps and w, one per row; coef, the sampling model's coefficients; diag, a named vector (ntrial, ntarget, smd, dmean, gindex, ess); bal, a data frame (var, target, trial, wtrial, smd, wsmd); and target.

Details

With target = "generalize" the target is the population the trial was drawn from, all the rows, and a trial unit's weight is 1 / ps; with "transport" it is the units outside the trial, and the weight is the odds (1 - ps) / ps (Stuart et al. 2011; Westreich et al. 2017; Tipton and Hartman 2023, eq. 3.11-3.12). Rows outside the trial have weight 0.

The diagnostics: smd, the difference of the mean logits of the scores between the trial and the target over their standard deviation in the target (Stuart et al. 2011); dmean, the difference of the mean scores; gindex, Tipton's (2014) generalisability index, the sum over bins equal-width bins of the scores of the square root of the trial's share times the target's, 1 when they are spread alike and 0 when they never meet (above 0.9 is very high, below 0.5 low); ess, Kish's effective number of trial units under the weights. bal gives each covariate's mean in the target and in the trial, unweighted and weighted, with the standardised differences from the target (over its standard deviation in the target).

References

Stuart, E. A., Cole, S. R., Bradshaw, C. P. and Leaf, P. J. (2011). The use of propensity scores to assess the generalizability of results from randomized trials. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series A, 174(2), 369-386. doi:10.1111/j.1467-985X.2010.00673.x

Tipton, E. (2014). How generalizable is your experiment? An index for comparing experimental samples and populations. Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics, 39(6), 478-501. doi:10.3102/1076998614558486

Westreich, D., Edwards, J. K., Lesko, C. R., Stuart, E. and Cole, S. R. (2017). Transportability of trial results using inverse odds of sampling weights. American Journal of Epidemiology, 186(8), 1010-1014. doi:10.1093/aje/kwx164

Tipton, E. and Hartman, E. (2023). Generalizability and transportability. In Zubizarreta, J. R., Stuart, E. A., Small, D. S. and Rosenbaum, P. R. (eds), Handbook of Matching and Weighting Adjustments for Causal Inference, ch. 3. Chapman and Hall/CRC. doi:10.1201/9781003102670

Examples

set.seed(8)
n <- 600
d <- data.frame(age = rnorm(n, 35, 10), prior = rpois(n, 1.5))
d$s <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-1 + 0.04 * (d$age - 35) + 0.3 * d$prior))
g <- gensw(d, "s", c("age", "prior"), target = "transport")
g
#> gensw: 223 trial units to transport to 377; logit SMD 0.47, Tipton's index 0.96, effective size 183.7
#>    var target  trial wtrial    smd      wsmd
#>    age 33.012 36.075 32.979 0.3000 -0.003267
#>  prior  1.358  1.771  1.317 0.3693 -0.036677
g$bal
#>     var   target    trial    wtrial       smd         wsmd
#> 1   age 33.01239 36.07538 32.979032 0.2999789 -0.003266946
#> 2 prior  1.35809  1.77130  1.317055 0.3693281 -0.036677349
